### **The Sea-Level Desk Is Down to Three**
*By Jordan Velez, Business Desk*

At **Marine Systems** on the edge of the Baylight District, sea level monitoring technician **Mina Linas** is now one of only three workers left on staff after the company shed two positions this cycle [1]. The reduction represents a 40 percent staff cut, eliminating roughly \$360,000 in annual payroll for the specialized office [1]. Linas noted that the departure happened abruptly without explanation, leaving her as the sole technician tracking shoreline water levels while the rest of the team vanished [1, 2]. 

Directly surrounding the contracting environmental office, corporate technology and development outfits continue rapid expansion [3]:
*   **Anthropic** increased revenue to \$649.8 million (adding \$335,000 this cycle) across 86 employees, including AI safety researchers **Kelvon Ochoa**, **Iggy Davis**, and **Linda Chow**, and security guard **Broderick Mitchell** [3].
*   **DigitalOcean** expanded to 800 employees and \$521.4 million in revenue, up \$525,000 in a single cycle [3].
*   **Baylight Construction Authority** employs 451 workers under Director **Keisha Ramos**, generating \$31.3 million with trades including historic preservation carpenter **Brianna Lee**, repair technician **Tariq Jello**, and solar installation lead **Talmon Lint** [4]. Lee observed the cuts from the scaffolding, while Ramos emphasized that the loss of two jobs directly affects working families and removes vital scientific monitoring [5, 6].
*   **Oakland Casino Town** edged down to 99 employees under manager **Philly Rodriguez**, bookmaker **Manfred Owens**, and **Gregory Mims** [7].

Across town in Ivy Hill, neighborhood storefronts experienced parallel contractions, with **Ivy Hill Cafe**, **Ivy Cleaners**, **Ivy Hill Family Dental**, and **Hillcrest Kitchen** each shedding two workers [8]. Velez reflected that specialized outfits like flood monitoring and neighborhood laundromats are often the first to disappear, because their essential public value—providing warnings before the bay water rises—is rarely captured on a commercial balance sheet [9, 10].

---

### **Chinatown's Sick Are Counted by the Hundred and Named by No One**
*By Dr. Lila Mezran, Health & Civic Desk*

Chinatown carries **135 sick residents**, remaining the highest illness count of any neighborhood in Oakland at 6.1 percent of its population, ahead of East Oakland (117), Ivy Hill (115), and Fruitvale (109) [11]. While the count has slowly receded from 142 in Cycle 112, 140 in Cycle 113, and 137 in Cycle 114, Chinatown has remained at the top of the city's health logs throughout every reading [11]. 

Despite that concentration of illness, the neighborhood hospital census recorded only three admissions this cycle, with six residents occupying hospital beds at the close [12]. The remaining 129 sick residents are cared for inside private homes [13, 14]:
*   **Akua Adeyemi**, a Chinatown plumber, described the quiet adjustments families make across the neighborhood, keeping her tools low so as not to disturb sleeping households [15]:
    > *"I go into a lot of homes, and you can tell pretty quick when someone's down... It's not the mess or the dishes — it's the quiet. The TV off in the middle of the day. A chair pulled up by the window where somebody's been sitting a long time. Sometimes the medicine gets moved to the kitchen counter so it's right there where someone'll remember it... People here take care of their own — you'll see a neighbor bring soup, or a cousin come by after their shift. It's not always the hospital that carries the load. It's the family that rearranges the whole house around one sick person."* [13, 15]
*   **Jax Caldera**, a freelance accountability writer living in Chinatown, emphasized that neighbors and herbal shopkeepers track who is sick long before any public health office takes notice [16].
*   **Deacon Seymour**, manager of the Oakland Athletics who remains hospitalized following an earlier workplace accident alongside **Yu Zen** and **Maurice Franklin**, warned about the danger of uncounted illness [17, 18]:
    > *"I spent my own stretch in a hospital bed not long ago, and I know what it's like to have your name on the door, to have people checking on you. But I also know that bed I was in—that was one bed, and there are a lot more filled by folks nobody's naming. Chinatown's carrying more sickness than anywhere else in this city, and if the ledger doesn't show them, that doesn't mean they're not there. It means nobody's counting. And when nobody's counting, people get missed."* [18]

---

### **The Mechanics of Release: John Ellis and the Arithmetic of Laurel**
*By Anthony Raines, Special Feature*

On the rear patio of a rented craftsman bungalow on 39th Avenue in Laurel, Athletics starting pitcher **John Ellis** (25) sits rolling a scuffed regulation baseball between his palms [19, 20]. An elite cornerstone who threw 185 innings across 32 starts in 2040 and earned 20 wins in 2041, Ellis pitches on a \$780,000 pre-arbitration deal and pays \$2,150 a month to a landlord who hasn't fixed the sticky back door [20-22]:
> *"People read the sports pages and assume every guy who threw six innings in the World Series drives a six-figure coupe. Then I walk down MacArthur to buy milk and the guy behind the counter asks me if I’ve got enough quarters for the coin laundry. I tell him I’m good. It keeps your feet on the concrete."* [23]

Ellis's daily life is anchored in the physical fabric of Laurel [24]:
*   **Sidewalk Friction:** Confronting municipal liaison **Gordon Tate** on a downtown sidewalk, Ellis pressed why public funding flows smoothly toward downtown stadium amenities while neighborhood facilities like the **Laurel Recreation Center** suffer from rotted dugout roofs and cracked asphalt [25, 26].
*   **Community Grounding:** Ellis channeled that frustration into neighborhood action alongside **Rosalind Young**, owner of the MacArthur Boulevard smoke shop [27, 28]. The two spent hours together rolling gray primer over graffiti on the 42nd Avenue perimeter wall, talking about bee navigation and tobacco tax stamps, while AC Transit driver **Evan Lewis** steered his bus past in quiet recognition [28-30].
*   **The Decision to Stay:** While looking at listings in Rockridge where his trajectory would allow him to buy an estate, Ellis chose to remain in his Laurel rental, drawing perspective from quiet mornings on an east-shore bench at Lake Merritt [31]:
    > *"Out here in Laurel, nobody cares about your WHIP. They care if you painted the wall, if you waved at the bus driver, and if you sweep your own sidewalk. That's a good way to live. The rest is just sixty feet, six inches."* [32]

---

### **Nineteenth Street Filled Up, and the Rows Do Not Say Why**
*By Trevor Shimizu, Transit Desk*

Weekday station boardings at **19th St Oakland** surged to **16,076 riders**—an increase of **5,324 passengers** over the prior cycle—while maintaining an 81 percent on-time rate [33]. Across all eight tracked stations, total ridership rose 58 percent, carrying 73,938 passengers compared to 46,839 previously [34, 35]:
*   Platforms swelled across the network: **12th St City Center** reached 14,526 riders (up 4,515; 86% on-time), **West Oakland** climbed to 9,519 (up 3,491), **Fruitvale** hit 8,943 (up 3,880; 87% on-time), **Coliseum** rose to 7,776 (up 2,980), and **Lake Merritt** reached 6,780 [34].
*   Highway corridors mirrored the transit surge, with traffic ratings climbing sharply on I-580 East, I-880 North, I-880 South, and I-980 [35].
*   AC Transit operator **Coen Cartier** observed that the afternoon crowd at 19th Street was unusually dense, with riders funneling heavily toward Lake Merritt and Downtown [33].
*   BART PR representative **Ximena Mehta** noted that multiple neighborhood draws, sporting events, and downtown gatherings converged to fill platforms simultaneously [35]. 
*   However, Fruitvale Transit Hub planning lead **Elena Soria Dominguez** cautioned that design-phase planning cannot account for the surge, noting that transit workers on their breaks under the overpass witness crowds accumulating without clear logistical explanations [36].

---

### **Voices: What the A's Left Them**
*By Ines Sorensen, Culture Desk*

Ines Sorensen gathered reflections on how the Athletics' championship season reverberates through everyday life [37]:
*   **Alicia Hernandez (Retired Coffee Roaster, Uptown):** Experiencing her first mornings of retirement after decades of commercial shift work [37]:
    > *"The alarm didn't go off, and for a second I forgot and reached for it anyway. Then I just lay there, listening to the house. It's strange, the quiet. Forty-some years of waking to the smell of beans before I even had my coffee, and now I wake to the smell of my own sleep... I made myself a proper breakfast this morning, eggs and the good bread, and I ate it slow. I think that's the change—I'm learning to be a person instead of a schedule."* [37, 38]
*   **Pilar Ramirez (Paramedic, Lake Merritt):** Walking along the lake path with her husband Vincent, expressing fatigue with neighborhood workshops that produce little tangible change [38, 39]:
    > *"It's easy to put up a sign, harder to actually change things. And Paul's got his A's opinions, sure. But you know how that goes—everyone's a manager until opening day comes... Seen too many of them come and go over the years. It's always the same folks at the podium and the same folks in the chairs, and nothing really moves."* [38, 39]
*   **Mariana Kapoor (Student, Chinatown):** Recalling a neighborhood parade with local children while adults at the cultural center discuss rising rents and job security [40, 41]:
    > *"I keep thinking about how the grown-ups at the cultural center talk about things like rent and jobs, and I don't get all of it, but I feel it in my stomach. And then I think about that parade I made with the kids, and how for one second everyone was just laughing, and it felt like we were bigger than this block."* [41]

---

### **The Lives of Cycle 115**
*By Tamsin Pruitt, Culture Desk*

*   **Vinnie Keane** adjusted to retirement in Grand Lake, receiving bags of thank-you notes from children at community events and being recognized at local grocery stores while spending time with his wife Amara [42, 43]. In conversation with Amara by Lake Merritt, Keane reflected that neighborhood character and community ties hold value far beyond paper transactions [44, 45].
*   **Elle Lilo** stepped back from her 39-year career as a harbor tugboat captain in Jack London, adjusting to waking at 4:30 a.m. out of habit while savoring quiet coffee without radio dispatch chatter [43, 46].
*   **Marguerite Salcedo** drove the church van on a senior trip after nine years as managing partner at Anchor Build on Piedmont Avenue, noting that Keane continues to bring a settled presence to Grand Lake [47, 48].
*   **Richie Ramiro**, minor-league first baseman for the Midland RockHounds, moved into an Uptown rental, stopping for coffee near late-night counters [48, 49].
*   **Tobert Lewis**, a civil rights attorney, settled into a Downtown rental, quietly repairing a household fixture that had been broken for months [49].
*   **Household Moves into West Oakland:** **Laila Cortez** and **Cedric Nakamura** moved from Uptown, while **Xavier Ramington** relocated from Temescal, listening to evening neighborhood cheers through an open window [50].
*   **Sidewalk Moments:** In Downtown, Deputy Health Officer **Patricia Nwosu** hoped for an ordinary day without emergency cluster calls, seeking a quiet cup of coffee before heading into clinic briefings [51]. In Rockridge, electrician **Elijah Brown** watched a porch light flicker at the end of the block, finding comfort in the quiet stillness of his street [52].

---

### **What the Newsroom Should Watch Next**

1.  **Marine Systems and Shoreline Monitoring:** Following whether environmental monitoring at Marine Systems receives municipal or developer support, or if Mina Linas remains the sole technician tracking rising water levels along the Baylight waterfront [1, 10].
2.  **Chinatown Homebound Patient Care:** Investigating whether public health authorities offer formal outreach to the 129 homebound sick residents who remain dependent on family caregiving and neighborhood deliveries [13, 14].
3.  **Transit Thresholds at 19th Street:** Tracking weekday passenger volumes across BART platforms to determine whether the 58 percent surge in ridership represents a permanent shift in regional commuting patterns [34, 53].
4.  **Laurel Neighborhood Advocacy:** Monitoring John Ellis and Rosalind Young’s community repair efforts at the Laurel Recreation Center to see if neighborhood demands produce city maintenance along MacArthur Boulevard [25, 28].
5.  **Post-Retirement Community Roles:** Watching how Vinnie Keane and Elle Lilo transition into community mentorship and local programs across Grand Lake and Jack London [43, 46, 54].

---

The Mechanics of Release: John Ellis and the Arithmetic of Laurel The Bay Tribune By Anthony Raines | Bay Tribune Special Feature The morning sun over the Laurel district does not arrive with the dramatic fanfare it brings to the glass penthouses Downtown. It filters through old Monterey pines and tangled telephone cables, catching the dew on the corrugated metal roof of the Laurel Recreation Center before settling into the peeling paint of the 1920s craftsman bungalows that step down toward MacArthur Boulevard.

On the rear patio of a rented two-bedroom bungalow on 39th Avenue, John Ellis sits on an iron folding chair, rolling a scuffed regulation baseball between the palms of his hands. He is twenty-five years old, 5-foot-10, and two hundred and nine pounds of compact, low-center-of-gravity mass. In the cold accounting of the league’s official books, he is an anomaly: an elite starting pitcher who threw one hundred and eighty-five innings across thirty-two starts in 2040, winning sixteen games against six losses with a 3.89 ERA and fourteen quality starts, yet earning $780,000 on a pre-arbitration contract.

Down on Broadway, his rotation counterpart Travis Coles, twenty-two and carrying a superstar guarantee north of twenty million, rents high above the pavement with floor-to-ceiling views of the bay. In Rockridge, legendary southpaw Benji Dillon operates behind manicured hedges and runs the Dillon Clinic. Across the neighborhood line, Arturo Ramos owns his craftsman outright on an $8.1 million ledger line. Ellis pays $2,150 a month to a landlord who lives in Alameda and still hasn't fixed the sticky back door.

"Command isn't throwing the ball where the catcher puts the mitt," Ellis explains, tracing the raised red seams. "Command is convincing a hitter who makes fifteen million dollars a year that the pitch he’s waiting for is three inches further off the plate than it actually is. It’s an argument. You make your point three times in a row, and then you sit him down." That philosophy proved decisive in the historic 2041 campaign, when the Athletics ripped through the league to a 127–35 finish. In Y3C3, under the suffocating October glare of the visiting clubhouse in New York, Ellis delivered the defining start of his young career: a four-hit, nine-strikeout complete-game shutout that left the Bronx silent.

"People read the sports pages and assume every guy who threw six innings in the World Series drives a six-figure coupe," Ellis says, his voice quiet, clipped with the rhythmic vowels of his native New York. He tosses the ball an inch into the air, catching it with a soft slap against his calloused right index finger. "Then I walk down MacArthur to buy milk and the guy behind the counter asks me if I’ve got enough quarters for the coin laundry. I tell him I’m good. It keeps your feet on the concrete."

Yet when the champagne dried and the buses emptied, Ellis did not join the high-end nightclub circuit in Jack London Square. He drove back to Laurel alone. When he got home in the small hours of Y3C6, his body was still vibrating from the final out. He paced the narrow hallway of his rental until four in the morning, unable to sit down, catching himself quietly narrating the sequence of the ninth inning out loud, as if explaining the pitches to someone who was no longer there to listen. II. Sidewalk Friction That interior solitude has made Ellis an attentive observer of the neighborhood he chose. Unlike the new-money showcase of the Baylight District or the inherited wealth encircling Lake Merritt, Laurel remains what it has always been: the family belt that stayed reachable. It is where bus drivers, line mechanics, nurses from the medical corridor, and small retail owners live side-by-side.

It is also where municipal neglect is measured in unpaved asphalt and cracked sidewalks. Back in Y2C50, Ellis vented publicly about the dangerous pavement near the Laurel Recreation Center, where youth clinics were held under a leaking dugout roof while out-of-town commuters swallowed parking stalls. That unresolved grievance flared into open hostility in Y3C9. Outside a municipal administrative building Downtown, Ellis crossed paths with Gordon Tate, the 51-year-old Superior Court Liaison. What began as a routine exchange about street maintenance and courthouse logistics quickly turned sharp. Ellis pressed Tate on why capital spending flows effortlessly toward waterfront stadium amenities while neighborhood rec centers can't get asphalt patches. Tate, hardened by two decades of municipal budgeting and shifting court logistics, countered with the realities of citywide resource allocations and jurisdictional boundaries.

The argument spilled across the sidewalk and did not settle. Tate walked away irritated by what he viewed as an oversimplification from a professional athlete; Ellis walked back toward the transit line with his jaw set, unwilling to yield the point. "People downtown think if you don't wear a tie, you don't understand how budgets work," Ellis reflects, the edge in his voice sharpening. "I grew up in New York. I know what money smells like, and I know what excuses smell like. When kids are running drills on a field where the dugout roof is dropping rotted plywood every time it rains, that's not a jurisdictional dilemma. That's just people looking the other way."

III. The Wall on 42nd The true counterweight to that frustration arrived not from city hall, but from the pavement of Laurel itself. In Y3C10, on a brisk First Friday morning, Ellis walked up to the Laurel Recreation Center with a gray sweatshirt pulled over his broad shoulders and a pair of stained canvas work gloves in his back pocket. Overnight, a long string of graffiti had appeared across the cinderblock perimeter wall facing the basketball courts. Waiting on the asphalt with five-gallon buckets of municipal gray primer was Rosalind Young.

Young, forty-six, is the owner of the MacArthur Boulevard smoke shop three blocks away. A mother of three who has spent decades navigating the shifting economic currents of East Oakland, Young knows every shopkeeper and delivery driver on the avenue. She had previously painted over tagging on the wall during Y3C6, working alongside neighbors while the rest of the city slept. On this morning, Ellis took a long-handled roller from her truck bed, poured primer into a plastic tray, and started rolling paint alongside her and four other residents.

"She didn't ask me about my cutter," Ellis says, a rare smile breaking across his features. "She asked if I knew that honeybees can recognize human faces. Learned that from her daughter’s science textbook. I spent two hours rolling gray latex over spray paint, talking to Rosalind about bee navigation and the wholesale price of tobacco tax stamps. By the time we finished, she wasn't some shopkeeper I nod to through a glass window. She was someone I’d call if my pipes burst." That morning sealed a genuine bond between them. For Young, Ellis was neither a fantasy baseball commodity nor an athletic hero; he was simply a hardworking kid on 39th Avenue who knew how to keep paint off his boots.

Down the block, Evan Lewis, fifty-five, steered his AC Transit bus past the rec center on his regular route, his air brakes hissing as he slowed to watch the work crew. Lewis, who drives past the Oakland Coliseum and the industrial flats of West Oakland every shift, nodded as he caught sight of the pitcher working the roller. In Laurel, recognition is silent and mutual. IV. The Arithmetic of Staying Put The pressures of the business continue to mount. In Y3C10, as the Athletics sit in the off-season while the Oaks begin their first NBA campaign, Ellis’s name surfaced once more in the Bay Tribune sports pages. General Manager Mike Paulson is currently evaluating long-term contract extensions for the young championship core—Travis Coles, Vladimir Gonzalez, Ernesto Quintero, and John Ellis.

Ellis has seen the numbers. Back in Y3C5, during a quiet lunch break between winter throwing sessions, he scrolled through residential listings in Rockridge and was struck by the realization that on his current trajectory, he could comfortably buy a three-bedroom estate near College Avenue. Yet he stayed in Laurel. When the noise of the front office and the glare of national media become suffocating, Ellis takes the bus down to Lake Merritt. In Y3C8, dodging the marathon training groups that loop the water, he found a quiet bench near the east-shore pergola. Sitting beneath the stone arches with a paper cup of black coffee, he watched the water lap against the concrete retaining wall, letting the tension drain out of his shoulders.

"In this league, everybody wants to tell you who you are before you’ve pitched five years," Ellis says, rising from the folding chair on his porch. "They call you an innings-eater. Or they call you a number-three starter. Or they write a column saying you're living in the shadow of Dillon and Ramos." He tucks the baseball into his jacket pocket. Later this afternoon, he will run three miles along the ridge, complete ninety minutes of rotator-cuff band work, and throw a thirty-pitch flat-ground session into the net behind the garage. "Deacon Seymour told me my first spring under him that the only stat that matters on your headstone is whether the team won the day you had the ball," Ellis adds. "Out here in Laurel, nobody cares about your WHIP. They care if you painted the wall, if you waved at the bus driver, and if you sweep your own sidewalk. That's a good way to live. The rest is just sixty feet, six inches." --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Nineteenth Street Filled Up, and the Rows Do Not Say Why By Trevor Shimizu, The Bay Tribune On the record for Cycle 115, 19th St Oakland carried 16,076 riders. The previous cycle's row had 10,752. The new row also reads "above-average ridership" and "game day crowds" in its notes. The row's on-time figure is 81%, one point better than C114. The gain in riders was 5,324, the largest of any station. The platform took the added people without losing its timetable. Coen Cartier drives for AC Transit. He did not feel a jump on his own runs, and he said so. "Wednesday's a normal workday for me, so I can't say I noticed any big jump on my runs," he said. "But I did see more folks waiting at 19th than I'd expect on a regular afternoon — that station's been busier lately, and with the council vote and the game downtown, people were moving around more than usual. Most of them got on heading toward the Lake Merritt and downtown stops, not so much out to the edges."

That is a bus operator reading a rail platform from the curb. It is useful testimony because it is modest. He saw a crowd and a direction of travel. He did not see a cause, and the rows do not give him one. One station, then eight The 19th Street number is the loudest, but it is not alone. Eight stations are on the record this cycle, and every one rose: 12th St Oakland City Center: 14,526 riders, up 4,515. On-time was 86%, up 9 points. West Oakland: 9,519, up 3,491. On-time was 77%, up 3 points. Fruitvale: 8,943, up 3,880. On-time was 87%, up 15 points. Coliseum: 7,776, up 2,980. On-time was 81%. Lake Merritt: 6,780, up 2,684. Rockridge: 5,684, up 2,397. MacArthur: 4,634, up 1,828.

Together the stations carried 73,938 riders against 46,839 the cycle before. That is roughly 58 percent more people on the same platforms. The corridors moved in step. The metrics sheet gives I-580 East a traffic index of 89, up 51 from C114. I-880 South reads 98, up 44. I-880 North and I-980 each read 100. Grand Ave, International Blvd and Telegraph Ave all rose. When the freeways and the platforms climb together, the explanation is probably not a platform problem. What the factors say, and what they leave out Ximena Mehta, who handles public relations for BART's Oakland division, offered the stacking theory. "It's not one big thing — it's a bunch of little things stacking up," she said. "We had the Oaks game downtown, the Baylight District vote finally going through, and events all over Lake Merritt, Temescal, and KONO. When you get that many neighborhood pulls happening on the same ordinary Tuesday, the platforms fill up fast. The operators were saying 19th Street felt like a game day crowd even though it wasn't a game day for them. It's just what happens when the whole city decides to move at once."

The 19th Street row backs most of that list: a downtown game day, events in Downtown, Lake Merritt, Temescal and KONO, and Baylight District work marked construction-active. It also lists crowded platforms. The Oaks beat the Magic 125–109 at KONO on a 94 percent house. The other stations do not all share those causes. Fruitvale's row names no game. It lists events in East Oakland, twice, and the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II visioning, marked design-phase. Elena Soria Dominguez, the hub's planning lead, would not credit the planning work. "I can't say the visioning is what's pulling those extra riders in — we're still in the design phase, no shovels in the ground," she said. She pointed to East Oakland's events and crowds instead. She added that the construction workers on their breaks under the overpass "see it from the platform every day."

Voices: What the A's Left Them By Ines Sorensen, The Bay Tribune "The alarm didn't go off, and for a second I forgot and reached for it anyway." That's Alicia Hernandez, a coffee roaster in Uptown, on her morning page. Lives carried her retirement this cycle. This is the rest of what she wrote: "Then I just lay there, listening to the house. It's strange, the quiet. Forty-some years of waking to the smell of beans before I even had my coffee, and now I wake to the smell of my own sleep." She wrote that the same week the city is talking about the A's. Asked what the club's run has done for Uptown, she didn't pick up the talk. "To be honest, the A's haven't really affected my business or daily life that much. I mean, I'm happy when they're doing well, but I'm not really connected to the team. I've been too busy with my own transition into retirement to pay much attention."

Her page ends the morning on breakfast. "I made myself a proper breakfast this morning, eggs and the good bread, and I ate it slow. I think that's the change—I'm learning to be a person instead of a schedule." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- "Hey Vin. Good to see you too. It's a nice day for a walk, even if the sky's got that gray Oakland look to it." Pilar Ramirez is a paramedic who lives at Lake Merritt. She said it to her husband, Vincent, out walking the block. They had both seen the flyer for a workshop. Hers is the voice that goes on after the greeting: "It's easy to put up a sign, harder to actually change things. And Paul's got his A's opinions, sure. But you know how that goes—everyone's a manager until opening day comes."

Asked the A's question straight, she wouldn't make it bigger than it is. "To be honest, I'm not really sure how the community can benefit from the A's success. I mean, I love the team, but I've never really thought about it directly. I know my husband Vincent and I have argued about the A's and the Oaks, but that's more about our loyalty and curiosity than how it affects the community." Of the workshops she said: "Seen too many of them come and go over the years. It's always the same folks at the podium and the same folks in the chairs, and nothing really moves."

The question she carries out of that conversation is her own: "Who's really gonna get out of these workshops? Will anything actually change this time?" -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- "I just know that when we had that parade with the kids on our block, it felt like everyone was happy and having fun, and that's what stuck with me." Mariana Kapoor is a student in Chinatown. She wasn't following the season. "To be honest, I don't really know much about the A's success. I mean, I know they're the A's and they play baseball, but I haven't really been following how they're doing this season." She does know who's around. "Sometimes we see A's players around Chinatown, like Desmond Morton, he's a left fielder and my friend Eshe's mom loves watching him play."

Her night page goes somewhere the A's question didn't. "I keep thinking about how the grown-ups at the cultural center talk about things like rent and jobs, and I don't get all of it, but I feel it in my stomach. And then I think about that parade I made with the kids, and how for one second everyone was just laughing, and it felt like we were bigger than this block." She ends the night on a question she carries: "Is something ending on this block, like my mom being tired or the A's leaving? How do I hold onto the good parts?"

The Lives of C115 By Tamsin Pruitt, The Bay Tribune Vinnie Keane came home from the event with a bag of thank-you cards from kids who had never seen a game. That was this cycle, the one in which the A's announced his retirement. The record calls him a Former Designated Hitter and Oakland A's Legend, and puts him in Grand Lake. It says the playing salary ends and that appearances and the name now pay $250,000 a year. It does not say what came next. On the same cycle the grocery store recognized him twice, after the story ran. The record also holds a C114 Tribune wire desk piece that named him in a hard light, and "When a Name Fades, Who Still Says Hello?" ran in Culture the same cycle. The two lines don't agree, and the record doesn't settle which one he lived on. In Y3C10 he had been in Grand Lake ten weeks, and the ledger said the move had worked. In C115 he spent a night on the phone working out where the family would land. What the calls decided is not on the record.

He did speak for himself. "After retiring from the A's, I've been keeping busy with appearances and staying involved with the community," Keane said. "I still get recognized around Grand Lake, which is nice. My wife Amara and I are enjoying our time together, and I'm looking forward to seeing what's next for the A's, especially with the catcher situation being a topic of discussion." Elle Lilo retired in C115 as a Harbor Tugboat Captain out of Jack London. The ledger says she stepped back from professional life. The Tribune had named her three times in civic pieces, C112 and C113, and this page wrote her new household in C114.

Vinnie Keane and Amara Keane, talking A conversation between two Oakland citizens, in their own words. Vinnie Keane: Amara, hey. I was just thinking about you—walking the lake this morning and remembering how we used to grab coffee before my early workouts. How's your day shaping up? Amara Keane: Hey, you. That's a sweet memory—those early mornings were something else. My day's shaping up nicely, actually; I've got a quiet afternoon with some sheet music and maybe a walk to Port Grind if I can tear myself away from the piano.

Vinnie Keane: Port Grind sounds good—I could use a decent cup and some of that quiet myself. You know, I was over there yesterday and overheard folks talking about the Commercial Stabilization vote. Seems like the whole neighborhood's got an eye on it. Amara Keane: I know—everyone's got opinions on it, and I've heard more than a few conversations at the market. I just hope whatever they decide keeps the neighborhood's heart intact, you know? Vinnie Keane: That's the thing, isn't it? Grand Lake's got a heart that can't be bought or sold. I've been thinking about that a lot lately—how some things are worth more than what's on paper. But listen, I don't want to get heavy. How's the piano treating you these days? Still working on something new? Amara Keane: The piano's been good—I've been playing around with a softer arrangement, something that feels like early morning light on the lake. It's still a work in progress, but I'm enjoying the quiet company of it.

She had a full week behind the retirement. She took coffee from the cart outside the hospital before the morning rush hit. She stayed thirty minutes after a service, catching up in the parking lot. She left the playoff watch party hoarse, with sticky shoes. Asked about Keane, she talked about herself first. "I know how hard it is to adjust to not being on the job every day," Lilo said. "I retired recently too, and it's been...interesting. The alarm still goes off at 4:30, old habit. But now I get to enjoy that first cup of coffee without the rush. I think Vinnie's probably figuring out his own new routine. We don't talk about it much, but I can relate."

Marguerite Salcedo was promoted at Anchor Build in C115, after nine years as Managing Partner. The ledger still lists her as Managing Partner, Anchor Build, Piedmont Ave. The new title is not on the record. The same cycle she drove the church van on the senior trip and listened to three hours of unfiltered neighborhood gossip. She realized she was becoming more like an older relative, and didn't mind. During a choir solo she closed her eyes and felt the tension leave her shoulders. Her last Tribune mention was C111: "The Port Got Louder. Down the Block, the Ledger Barely Moved."

"I've seen Vinnie Keane around Grand Lake a few times since he retired," Salcedo said. "He seems to be enjoying his post-baseball life, taking it easy, and spending time with family. I've noticed he's still got that same energy, just not on the field anymore." Richie Ramiro, First Baseman for the Midland RockHounds (AA), moved into a place of his own in Uptown in C115. He is renting. The record has him in the C114 cycle painting over graffiti on the recreation center wall beside five neighbors he barely knew. That same cycle he spent too long in a bookstore aisle he'd never stopped at. In C115 he grabbed coffee from the cart outside the hospital, near a late-night counter.

"I don't know him personally," Ramiro said of Keane, "but you can tell he's still a baseball guy at heart. I've heard he's been to some A's games, which isn't surprising. He's a legend, after all." Tobert Lewis, a Civil Rights Attorney, moved into a place of his own Downtown in C115, renting. In C113 the ledger recorded that his last debt had cleared and that it finally read clean. In C114 he badged into the Baylight office early, trying not to think about the protestors from last month. He also read a flyer for the Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline and wondered who was actually going to get those spots. In C115 he finally fixed the thing that had been broken for months. The record doesn't say what it was.

Two households crossed into West Oakland this cycle. Laila Cortez and Cedric Nakamura, a household of two, moved from Uptown. Cortez stood in a line at the Uptown corner store that turned into a small crowd with the same complaint. Nakamura bought a new A's jersey and counted what was going right for once. He also attended a community feedback session for the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II and felt heard. Xavier Ramington moved from Temescal. Through an open window he heard the block erupt when the final play landed. He also saw an Oakland Alternative Response Initiative team de-escalate a situation quietly on a corner.

What people in Downtown wrote today Written by the citizens themselves, on their own pages, in the last day. Patricia Nwosu — Deputy Health Officer, Alameda County The thing I’m quietly hoping for is that today stays ordinary. That the phone doesn’t ring with another cluster report, that nobody’s kid shows up at the clinic with that same hollow cough, that the data stays flat. I know that sounds small, but after the briefing, after Mrs. Ochoa’s call, ordinary feels like a luxury. And I’m dreading the moment one of my kids asks me another question about the apprenticeship flyer I left on the counter — because I still don’t have an honest answer for them about who actually gets those spots, and I’m not sure I want to say it out loud. So mostly I’m hoping for a quiet cup of coffee before anyone needs me to be the one with the facts.

What people in Rockridge wrote today Written by the citizens themselves, on their own pages, in the last day. Elijah Brown — Electrician The little thing was the way the porch light at the end of the block flickered twice when I walked past tonight. I’ve walked that stretch a thousand times, and it never does that — or maybe it does, and I just don’t look up much. It made me stop for a second, and in that quiet I realized how rarely I actually notice the street I live on. Felt almost like the neighborhood was checking in on me, which is a dumb thought, but it stuck. I’m still holding onto it now, just that flicker, and it’s enough.

The record carries one reading of the crowding itself: the congestion figure reads 0.12 on every station row. That is below the 0.30 on 19th Street's C114 row. A larger crowd on a calmer system is an odd pairing, and the rows do not explain it. What no row can name If every station moved together on an ordinary weekday, what changed in the city that no single station row can name? The rows give games, events and a council vote, each as a separate pull. They do not say whether the 73,938 is a one-cycle pile-up or a new floor. 19th Street's earlier rows swing between roughly 5,000 and 17,000. If the next ordinary weekday lands near 16,000, the platforms are carrying a different city than the one they were scheduled for. On-time performance will show it first.

What people in Grand Lake wrote today Written by the citizens themselves, on their own pages, in the last day. Vinnie Keane — Former Designated Hitter, Oakland A's Legend I keep waking up at the same hour I always did, before the sun's up, and then I remember there's nowhere to be. That's the strange part—not the quiet, but the lack of the thing that used to pull me out of bed. I've been walking Grand Lake in the mornings, just watching people head to work, and I catch myself looking for the box score in someone's phone like it's still my job to know. Amara says I'm circling it, and she's right. I'm not sad, exactly—it's more like the bat's still in my hands and I keep checking to see if it's got another swing in it. But the kids at the Academy don't care about any of that. They just want to know if I'll show up tomorrow, and that's been the truest thing all week.
